## yetone/magpie (https://github.com/yetone/magpie)
Description: Pool every plan you pay for — Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, GLM Coding Plan, Kimi Code and more — and use them in any agent: Claude Code, Codex, Claude Desktop… When one runs out, the next takes over.

Language: Go; license: MIT; created 2026-09-23; last push 2026-11-26

README (start):
# magpie

### All your plans, one pool. Any agent.

**Claude Code on your ChatGPT Pro. Codex on your Claude Max. Claude Desktop on your GLM Coding Plan.**
Add every plan you pay for once, and every agent can use all of them.
No plan stays locked to the agent you bought it for, and when one runs out, the next takes over.

[](https://github.com/yetone/magpie-releases/releases/latest) [](https://github.com/yetone/magpie/stargazers) [](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF) [](LICENSE)
    

Thanks to [Kimi](https://usemagpie.ai/go/kimi/readme) for supporting magpie and the open source community.

Sponsors

  
  

**[Download](https://usemagpie.ai)**  ·  **[Docs](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/start)**  ·  **[Reference](docs/reference.md)**  ·  **[Plugins](https://github.com/magpie-community/plugins)**  ·  **[Discord](https://discord.gg/vGSnD3ZKQF)**  ·  **English** · [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md)

  
  

## Is magpie for you?

Each agent keeps its model in its own file, in its own format, with its own keys and base URLs. A subscription you pay for works in one agent and nowhere else. magpie puts all of that behind one app and one local gateway:

- **Pool every plan you pay for**: the Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini or Grok plan you're signed in to, a coding plan sold as a key (GLM, Kimi Code, Volcengine, Bailian, StepFun), pay-as-you-go keys and local models. Every agent can use every one of them.
- **Pick any model for any agent** from one list. magpie edits the one key that matters in the agent's own config.
- **Keep going when a quota runs out**: a provider's next account takes over, and a routing group moves on to another model or provider, so the agent never sees the error. With one account and no group there is nothing to move to, and the error reaches the agent.
- **Keep your secrets off the vendor's servers**: once you turn masking on in **Settings → Privacy** (it's off by default), keys, passwords and emails in a prompt are masked on your computer before the request leaves it, and put back in the reply.

It's for you if you use more than one agent, more than one provider, or more than one account. If you use one agent on its vendor's own plan and that's enough, you don't need it.

Runs on macOS, Windows and Linux (menu bar app, window, TUI, web UI and CLI), in Docker, and on Termux.

## Quick start

**1 · Install.** Download the app from **[usemagpie.ai](https://usemagpie.ai)**, or run:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://usemagpie.ai/install.sh | sh
```

Mac builds are signed and notarised, every release file carries a GitHub Actions build attestation (`gh attestation verify  -R yetone/magpie-releases`), and every build updates itself. On Linux the script installs the desktop app, and on a desktop without WebKitGTK 4.1 installs it first with your package manager (sudo asks for your password); with no desktop, or no terminal to ask at, it installs the terminal build and says which package to add. `--gui` or `--tui` chooses. Behind a firewall, use `--proxy` or `--mirror`. With Nix, `nix profile install github:yetone/magpie-releases` (`#magpie-cli` for the terminal build; Linux and Apple silicon Macs, updated with each release). Or `go install github.com/yetone/magpie@latest`, or the [Docker image](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/docker). Remove magpie with `curl -fsSL https://usemagpie.ai/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall`: it puts your agents back as they were, then takes off what the script installed (with magpie deleted already, it downloads one to put them back); your settings in `~/.config/magpie` stay unless you add `--purge`.

**2 · Add a provider.** Open magpie and go to **Providers → Add provider**. Pick a preset and paste a key, or sign in with a subscription.

**3 · Pick a model** for each agent on the **Agents** page. Start a new session and it's on the new model.

Or do it all from the terminal:

```sh
magpie provider add deepseek sk-…              # a preset needs only the key
magpie claude deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro          # Claude Code on DeepSeek
magpie codex moonshot/kimi-k2.5                 # Codex on Kimi
magpie group add "Opus anywhere" models=claude/claude-opus-5-5,copilot/claude-opus-5.5 routing=smart
magpie claude group/opus-anywhere               # fails over between subscriptions
magpie save work && magpie use work             # profiles
magpie quota                                    # what's left on every plan
magpie settings set theme dark                  # every Settings switch, from the terminal
magpie tool generate_image "a magpie, watercolour" -o hero.png   # magpie's image, vision and search tools, called directly
magpie tui                                      # the whole thing, in a terminal
```

magpie finds the subscriptions your agents are signed in to by reading their sign-ins (Claude Code's and Codex's files, the Keychain). To keep it from reading them, turn off Settings → Privacy → *Subscription accounts*, or run `magpie accounts discovery off` (`on` turns it back on). `MAGPIE_NO_ACCOUNTS=1` turns it off for one run without changing the saved setting. API-key providers work either way.

## Supported agents

Claude Code · Claude Desktop · Claude Science · Codex · Gemini CLI · Antigravity CLI · Dim · OpenCode · OpenChamber · MiMo Code · DevEco Code · Pi · oh-my-pi · StepCode · MothX · PenguinHarness · Aside · OmO · Prime Agent · mu · Goose · Cursor CLI · Cursor Private Inference · Zed · VS Code Chat · VS Code Insiders · VSCodium Chat · Zoo Code · JetBrains Air · Air (JetBrains IDEs) · Copilot (JetBrains) · Copilot CLI · Crush · DeepSeek Harness · Reasonix Studio · Command Code · fx · Devin · Hermes Agent · Mister Morph · Kimi Code · jcode · Mistral Vibe · Qwen Code · Muse Code · Empryo · nanobot · miniQ · Paimon · MiniMax Code · Droid · Cline · Qoder · Qoder CN · Grok Build · Kigi · Grok App · ZCode · WorkBuddy · WorkBuddy AI · CodeBuddy · Pencil · Paseo · OpenPencil · OpenBot · Craft Agents · Tuanjie Cowork · NewMax · LiveAgent · Raycast · Kiro Crew · OpenMausBot · T3 Code · OpenHanako · AtomCode · Open Code Review · Snow CLI · Alma · Shelley · Cindy · Lody · AionUi · Cherry Studio · Ante · AstrBot · QwenPaw · OpenClaw · Avibe · Kun · Nowledge Mem

magpie shows only the agents installed on your machine; setup notes for some of them are in the [reference](docs/reference.md#notes-on-some-agents). Anything else that takes a base URL can use the gateway too:

```sh
export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:3425/v1     OPENAI_API_KEY=magpie
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:3425     ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=magpie
export GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:3425 GEMINI_API_KEY=magpie
```

## How it fits together

The gateway at `127.0.0.1:3425` speaks OpenAI Chat, OpenAI Responses, Anthropic Messages and Gemini, and translates between them, streaming, tool calls and reasoning included.

  
  

## What it does

### Any model, any agent

Click a value and a searchable list opens: every model of every provider you added, as `provider/model`. The agent's config is rewritten atomically, and its comments, order and formatting stay as they were. **Profiles** save every agent's setup under one name ("Budget", "Focus") and switch them all back in one move. Each agent can also have its own short list of models; a profile keeps that list too.

  
  

  
  

### Privacy masking

Agents put what they read into the prompt: an `.env`, a config file, a log with a token in it. With masking on, magpie swaps those values for placeholders on your computer before a request leaves it, and swaps them back in the reply. Your agent and your files keep the real values; the vendor never sees them.

  
  

| | |
| :-- | :-- |
| **Found two ways** | Rules for what is certain (API keys, private keys, tokens, emails, and card and ID numbers whose checksum adds up), and, if you want it, a model that runs on this computer for the names, addresses and passwords no rule can find (a 1.6 GB download, on the CPU) |
| **Put back everywhere** | A value becomes a placeholder such as `{{API_KEY_k3v9x2mq}}`, and every placeholder in the reply turns back into its value: streamed text and tool-call arguments too, so a command the agent runs has the real key |
| **Nothing breaks** | A value gets the same placeholder every time, so the conversation, the prompt cache and thinking signatures stay valid. A value masked once is masked wherever it shows up later |
| **Never on disk** | Values are held in memory only. The record keeps each value's kind, length and first characters. If masking is on and can't run, the request is held back (503), never sent as written |
| **You can check it** | **Insights › Masking** lists every request it changed, with what the vendor got instead, side by side, and **Try it** in Settings shows what a text would become |
| **Your rules** | Secrets and personal data each on or off, finer kinds (passport, IBAN, MAC, public IP…), your own words and patterns, and whether a value found is masked, only warned about, or held back (**Mask**, **Warn**, **Block**) |

The cost: the model sees `{{API_KEY_…}}`, not the key, so a task about the value itself (why is this token refused?) can't be done on it. Put such values under **Never mask**. Rules can be wrong now and then; the Masking page is where you'd see it. It's off until you turn it on in **Settings → Privacy**. Emails at names kept for examples (`example.com`, `.test`, `.invalid`) are left as written.

### Providers

Pick a preset, paste a key. Model lists come from the vendor, with names and reasoning levels filled in from [models.dev](https://models.dev), so a model released this morning is in your picker on the next refresh.

> **Presets include** Anthropic · OpenAI · Google Gemini · Google Vertex AI · Amazon Bedrock (runtime and Mantle) · DeepSeek · Kimi · Zhipu GLM · MiniMax · StepFun · LongCat · Qwen · Baidu Qianfan · Tencent Cloud · Huawei Cloud MaaS · Volcengine Ark · Mistral · Voyage AI · Groq · Nous Portal · xAI · OpenRouter · Vercel AI Gateway · GMI Cloud · Together · Fireworks · Fireworks Nexus · SiliconFlow · NVIDIA NIM · ModelScope · Ollama · LM Studio … and any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible URL.

**Import** brings in the providers from CC Switch, Claude Code, Codex and Alma. **[Add to magpie](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/import)** links let a provider's website hand its config to magpie in one click. Each key and each account can go through a proxy of its own.

  
  

### Subscriptions

An agent you're signed in to is a subscription with models behind it, so magpie offers it as a provider to every other agent. Add several accounts per subscription and magpie fails over between them.

- **Claude**: drives the real local `claude` binary and bridges your agent's tools over MCP
- **Codex / ChatGPT**: your ChatGPT plan's models, in every other agent
- **GitHub Copilot**, **Gemini (Code Assist)**, **Antigravity** (through your own agy CLI), **Grok (SuperGrok)** and more
- **Any OpenCode auth plugin or pi package** from npm

**Daily warm-up** starts each Claude and ChatGPT account's 5-hour window at the times you choose, or the moment the last one resets.

### Routing groups

A **routing group** is several models an agent picks as one, such as `group/daily-coding`. The gateway spreads requests over every member's keys and accounts:

| Mode | What it does |
| :-- | :-- |
| **`smart`** | Of the subscriptions with quota left, use the one that renews soonest, so less is wasted at the reset |
| **`order`** | Use the first model until it can't answer, then the next |
| **`rotate`** | Move to the next member on each turn |
| **`usage`** | Use the least-used member first |
| **`pace`** | Use the account with the most of its week left per hour until it resets |

A conversation **stays with the account that answered it** while the vendor's prompt cache is worth keeping. Groups can contain groups. **[Intent routing](https://usemagpie.ai/docs/intent)** has a small mode

🚅 LiteLLM

---

## What is LiteLLM

LiteLLM is an open source AI Gateway that gives you a single, unified interface to call 100+ LLM providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, Azure, and more — using the OpenAI format.

Use it as a **Python SDK** for direct library integration, or deploy the **AI Gateway (Proxy Server)** as a centralized service for your team or organization.

[**Jump to LiteLLM Proxy (LLM Gateway) Docs**](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/simple_proxy) 
[**Jump to Supported LLM Providers**](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/providers)

---

## Why LiteLLM

Managing LLM calls across providers gets complicated fast — different SDKs, auth patterns, request formats, and error types for every model. LiteLLM removes that friction:

- **Unified API** — one interface for 100+ LLMs, no provider-specific SDK juggling
- **Drop-in OpenAI compatibility** — swap providers without rewriting your code
- **Production-ready gateway** — virtual keys, spend tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and an admin dashboard out of the box
- **8ms P95 latency** at 1k RPS ([benchmarks](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/benchmarks))

### OSS Adopters

  
    
    
    
    
    
    Netflix
    
  

---

## Features

LLMs - Call 100+ LLMs (Python SDK + AI Gateway)

[**All Supported Endpoints**](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/supported_endpoints) - `/chat/completions`, `/responses`, `/embeddings`, `/images`, `/audio`, `/batches`, `/rerank`, `/a2a`, `/messages` and more.

### Python SDK

```shell
uv add litellm
```

An independent `litellm-core` distribution provides the Python SDK with the same
`import litellm` API and runtime dependencies. It has no optional extras, CLI entry
points, or bundled dashboard. Install one SDK distribution per environment because
`litellm` and `litellm-core` own overlapping Python files. Use `litellm` for the
proxy, CLI, and optional extras

Build and install core from this checkout while its release integration is pending:

```shell
python litellm/scripts/build_core_distribution.py --out-dir dist/core
python -m pip install dist/core/litellm_core-*.whl
```

The builder requires Git, `uv` and the Rust build toolchain. It reads the release version
from the root `pyproject.toml`, leaves source files unchanged, and produces a wheel
and a self-contained sdist in `dist/core`. Run installation in a fresh environment
without `litellm`

```python
from litellm import completion
import os

os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"] = "your-openai-key"
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "your-anthropic-key"

# OpenAI
response = completion(model="openai/gpt-6.1-sol", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}])

# Anthropic  
response = completion(model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-20250514", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}])
```

### AI Gateway (Proxy Server)

[**Getting Started - E2E Tutorial**](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/docker_quick_start) - Setup virtual keys, make your first request

```shell
uv tool install 'litellm[proxy]'
litellm --model gpt-6.1-sol
```

```python
import openai

client = openai.OpenAI(api_key="anything", base_url="http://0.0.0.0:4000")
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-6.1-sol",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}]
)
```

Auto Routing - Choose a model for each prompt (Python SDK + AI Gateway)

### Python SDK

[**Docs: Autorouter SDK**](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/autorouter_sdk)

Install with `uv add litellm` and set `OPENAI_API_KEY` for the models below.

```python
import asyncio
from litellm import Router

router = Router(model_list=[
    {"model_name": "fast", "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/gpt-6-luna"}},
    {"model_name": "capable", "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/gpt-6.1-sol"}},
    {"model_name": "auto", "litellm_params": {
        "model": "auto_router/complexity_router",
        "complexity_router_config": {
            "classifier_type": "heuristic",
            "tiers": {"SIMPLE": "fast", "MEDIUM": "fast",
                      "COMPLEX": "capable", "REASONING": "capable"},
            "return_raw_model_name": True,
        },
        "complexity_router_default_model": "capable",
    }},
])
response = asyncio.run(router.acompletion(
    model="auto", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is 2+2?"}],
))
print(response.model, response.choices[0].message.content)
```

### AI Gateway (Proxy Server)

[**Create an Auto Router**](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/auto_router/setup), then call its model name. Replace `auto` and the URL below with yours, and set `LITELLM_API_KEY` to your virtual key.

```shell
curl http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $LITELLM_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"auto","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 2+2?"}]}'
```

A2A - Invoke A2A Agents (Python SDK + AI Gateway)

[**Supported Providers**](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/a2a#add-a2a-agents) - LangGraph, Vertex AI Agent Engine, Azure AI Foundry, Bedrock AgentCore, Pydantic AI

### Python SDK - A2A Protocol

```python
from litellm.a2a_protocol import A2AClient
from a2a.types import SendMessageRequest, MessageSendParams
from uuid import uuid4

client = A2AClient(base_url="http://localhost:10001")

request = SendMessageRequest(
    id=str(uuid4()),
    params=MessageSendParams(
        message={
            "role": "user",
            "parts": [{"kind": "text", "text": "Hello!"}],
            "messageId": uuid4().hex,
        }
    )
)
response = await client.send_message(request)
```

### AI Gateway (Proxy Server)

**Step 1.** [Add your Agent to the AI Gateway](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/a2a#adding-your-agent) — set `protocolVersion` to `1.0` or `0.3` per agent

**Step 2.** Call Agent via A2A SDK (requires `a2a-sdk>=1.1.0`)

```python
import httpx
from a2a.client import A2ACardResolver, ClientConfig, ClientFactory
from a2a.types import Message, Part, Role, SendMessageRequest
from a2a.utils.constants import TransportProtocol
from uuid import uuid4

base_url = "http://localhost:4000/a2a/my-agent"  # LiteLLM proxy + agent name
headers = {"Authorization": "Bearer "}    # LiteLLM master key or a virtual key

async with httpx.AsyncClient(headers=headers, timeout=60.0) as http_client:
    resolver = A2ACardResolver(httpx_client=http_client, base_url=base_url)
    agent_card = await resolver.get_agent_card()
    config = ClientConfig(
        httpx_client=http_client,
        streaming=False,
        supported_protocol_bindings=[TransportProtocol.JSONRPC, TransportProtocol.HTTP_JSON],
    )
    client = ClientFactory(config).create(agent_card)

    request = SendMessageRequest(
        message=Message(
            message_id=uuid4().hex,
            role=Role.ROLE_USER,
            parts=[Part(text="Hello!")],
        )
    )
    async for event in client.send_message(request):
        populated = event.ListFields()
        if populated and populated[0][0].name in ("message", "msg"):
            print("".join(getattr(p, "text", "") or "" for p in populated[0][1].parts))
```

from litellm import Harness, sandbox

result = litellm.agent(

---

# **🔥 Firecrawl**

**Knowledge infrastructure to make your agents smarter. 🔥** You can use Firecrawl three ways. This repo holds the code for Firecrawl Local and the self-hosted server, along with SDKs that work with all three.

- **[Firecrawl Local](#firecrawl-local).** Run Firecrawl on your own machine as one binary that turns websites into clean markdown, plugs into your AI agent as an MCP server and serves the Firecrawl API on localhost.
- **[Firecrawl Cloud](#firecrawl-cloud).** Use the hosted service at [firecrawl.dev](https://firecrawl.dev/?ref=github) for everything Local does at scale with nothing to run, plus search and the 550+ data providers in [Firecrawl Alexandria](https://alexandria.firecrawl.dev) for far more knowledge than scraping alone.
- **[Self-hosting](#self-hosting).** Deploy the full Firecrawl server from `apps/api` with its own queues, workers and databases on your own infrastructure.

_Pst. Hey, you, join our stargazers :)_

  

---

## Firecrawl Local

[Firecrawl Local](apps/local) scrapes, crawls and maps from your own machine without a database, queue or container, and it reaches Firecrawl Cloud when your AI agents need search or Alexandria. It installs from crates.io. You need Rust and a C compiler, which on macOS means `xcode-select --install` and on Debian or Ubuntu means `build-essential`.

```bash
cargo install firecrawl-local
```

If you don't have Rust, [Firecrawl Cloud](#firecrawl-cloud) runs the same scrape with nothing to build and no signup.

```bash
npx -y firecrawl-cli@latest scrape https://firecrawl.dev
```

Scrape a page and print its markdown.

```bash
firecrawl-local scrape https://firecrawl.dev --markdown
```

Crawl a site and save one markdown file per page.

```bash
firecrawl-local crawl https://docs.firecrawl.dev --limit 50 --out ./pages
```

List every URL on a site.

```bash
firecrawl-local map https://firecrawl.dev
```

Pages that need JavaScript render in the Chrome or Chromium already on your machine, and PDFs and Office documents are parsed locally too. Without a browser, static pages still work and a page that needed one comes back with a warning.

### Add it to your AI agent

`init` finds Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Gemini CLI and Codex on your machine and adds Firecrawl Local to each one as an MCP server. It backs up every config file first, and the MCP server itself needs Node.js 22 or newer.

```bash
firecrawl-local init
```

Restart your AI tool afterwards. Its scrape, crawl, map and batch scrape tools run on your machine, and the other Firecrawl tools go to Firecrawl Cloud.

### Run the Firecrawl API on localhost

`serve` answers the Firecrawl v2 API on port 3002, so code written for Firecrawl runs against it unchanged and local routes need no API key.

```bash
firecrawl-local serve
```

Point any Firecrawl SDK at it by setting the API URL.

```python
from firecrawl import Firecrawl

app = Firecrawl(api_url="http://localhost:3002")
print(app.scrape("https://firecrawl.dev").markdown)
```

The [Firecrawl Local README](apps/local) covers every command and option, the security defaults for `serve` and running it in Docker. Move to [Firecrawl Cloud](#firecrawl-cloud) when you need structured JSON, Interact, the Agent or scale beyond one machine.

---

## What runs where

| Feature | Firecrawl Local | Firecrawl Cloud |
|---------|-----------------|-----------------|
| [Scrape](#scrape) | Markdown, HTML, raw HTML and links | Adds structured JSON, summaries, screenshots and browser actions |
| [Crawl](#crawl), [Map](#map) and [Batch Scrape](#batch-scrape) | ✅ | ✅ |
| PDFs and Office documents | ✅ | ✅, plus [Parse](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/parse) for uploaded files |
| [Search](#search) | Through Firecrawl Cloud, no account needed | ✅ |
| [Alexandria](#alexandria) | Through Firecrawl Cloud after `firecrawl-local login` | ✅ |
| [Interact](#interact), [Agent](#agent) and [Monitor](https://docs.firecrawl.dev/features/monitoring) | | ✅ |

Scraping, crawling and mapping run on your machine. By default a single-page scrape that won't load there is fetched by Firecrawl Cloud instead and marked `"source": "firecrawl-cloud"` in the result. Those Cloud calls work without an account at a limited rate, and `firecrawl-local login` puts them on your Firecrawl account. Set `FIRECRAWL_CLOUD=off` to keep everything on your machine.

---

## Firecrawl Cloud

Firecrawl Cloud runs everything Firecrawl Local does at scale, with no browser or machine of your own to look after. It also gives your AI agents access to far more knowledge than scraping alone, with search, Alexandria, Interact and Agent all through a single API.

- **Works on the real web.** Covers 96% of the web, including JS-heavy pages and dynamic apps ([see benchmarks](https://www.firecrawl.dev/blog/the-worlds-best-web-data-api-v25)).
- **Fast.** P95 latency of 3.4s across millions of pages, built for real-time AI agents and dynamic apps.
- **LLM-ready output.** Clean markdo

URL: https://usemagpie.ai/docs/docker

magpie
Download
CONTENTS
Overview

DOCS · SERVERS

magpie in Docker

Run magpie on a server or a NAS that has no desktop: its gateway serves your models to agents on other computers, and you add providers and sign in to subscriptions from a page in your browser.

Image	ghcr.io/yetone/magpie, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64
Tags	latest (the newest release), daily (the desktop app's Daily channel: once a day at 20:00 UTC, the newest release whose CI run passed, or an urgent one at once), stable (the desktop app's Stable channel: a release a week, out three days first, or an urgent one at once), 0.1.1150 (one release), 0.1, edge (every change on main)
Ports	3425 the gateway agents call; 3430 the browser UI, when the container runs magpie web; it answers the gateway’s /v1 routes too, so a reverse proxy needs only this port
Volume	/config: providers, keys, sign-ins, plugins and usage
User	nonroot (uid 65532)

The image holds magpie’s terminal-only build on Debian 13 slim, with bash for a terminal in the container and curl for the installers of the CLIs some subscriptions sign in with (Cursor, Devin, Grok Build). It runs magpie serve (the gateway alone) unless given another command. The container finds no agents to wire, so magpie in it is a gateway: the agents that use it run elsewhere.

Run it

Run it with the browser UI, a key for that page you keep across restarts, and both ports on the host’s loopback only:

SHELL
Copy
docker run -d --name magpie --restart unless-stopped \
  -p 127.0.0.1:3425:3425 -p 127.0.0.1:3430:3430 \
  -e MAGPIE_WEB_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 16) \
  -v magpie-config:/config \
  ghcr.io/yetone/magpie:latest web --addr 0.0.0.0:3430 --no-open

docker logs magpie

The log names the page with its key:

OUTPUT
● magpie web on http://127.0.0.1:3430/?k=0f3c9a1e…
  on the network http://172.17.0.2:3430/?k=0f3c9a1e…
  these are the container's own addresses: other machines use the host's, and MAGPIE_PUBLIC_URL=http://<host>:<port> puts it here
  other containers on this host http://172.17.0.1:3425
! anyone with the link can change magpie and see its keys, and the network carries it unencrypted
  the link carries MAGPIE_WEB_KEY · gateway http://127.0.0.1:3425 · Ctrl-C to stop
Agents outside the container need a gateway key. In the container any key works. A request from the host or another machine is answered only with an enabled gateway key, and gets 401 without one: make one as in Gateway keys. 127.0.0.1: in -p keeps a port on the host; leave it out, or name the host’s LAN or VPN address, for other machines to reach it.

Without web --addr 0.0.0.0:3430 --no-open the container runs the gateway alone, which you then set up from a terminal in it (docker exec -it magpie magpie provider add …). A folder bind-mounted at /config works in place of the named volume, if uid 65532 can write it: sudo chown -R 65532:65532 /volume1/docker/magpie/config.

The browser UI

Open the link from the log. The key in it is traded for a cookie and taken out of the address; a page opened without it is turned away (401). With MAGPIE_WEB_KEY set (16 or more letters, digits or - . _ ~; openssl rand -hex 16 makes one) the key stays the same across restarts, and a browser stays signed in for 400 days. Without it, every start makes a new key: a browser stays signed in, closed and opened again too, until magpie starts again, and then needs the new link.

The page is in gateway mode: Providers, Gateway, Routing, Usage, Sessions, Plugins and Settings, with no Agents, since there are no agents in the container. Library has its MCP servers, with the MCP router: other computers’ apps connect at the router’s address with a gateway key. Beside them are its Skills and Instructions: a magpie on another computer that adds this one as an Another computer’s magpie provider, with Use its skills and prompts on, takes them and gives them to its own agents, since a skill is a folder on the agent’s computer. Sessions lists only the sessions of agents on other computers that came through this gateway, never this machine’s agents’ files. Settings → General → Gateway mode turns it off.

On a NAS or a server you reach over SSH, open the page through a tunnel rather than publishing 3430: ssh -L 3430:127.0.0.1:3430 you@nas, then the log’s link on your own computer.

Anyone with the link can change magpie and see its keys. Keep 3430 on loopback or a VPN. Across the network, serve it over HTTPS: give magpie a certificate with MAGPIE_TLS_CERT and MAGPIE_TLS_KEY, or put it behind a reverse proxy with TLS, such as Caddy.
Sign in to subscriptions

Add API keys on Providers as on the desktop. A subscription’s sign-in (ChatGPT, Claude…) opens the vendor’s page in your browser, and when you are done the vendor sends that browser back to localhost, for ChatGPT http://localhost:1455/auth/callback?code=…. That is your own computer, not the container, so the page doesn’t load. Copy its whole address from the address bar and paste it into the sign-in’s Callback URL field.

The same from a terminal:

SHELL
Copy
docker exec -it magpie magpie accounts add codex

Open the link it prints, sign in, then paste the address the browser ended on. The browser UI can also import sign-ins from a file.

A Claude subscription is signed in to and answered through Claude Code, which the image doesn’t have. Have magpie download Anthropic’s own build first: it says the version, where it comes from and where it goes, asks, and checks the download’s SHA-256 against Anthropic’s manifest. It is kept in /config/cache, on the volume, so a new image keeps it, and magpie keeps it at Claude Code’s newest release by itself: it looks a minute after it starts and every six hours, and downloads a newer one the same way. Nothing needs installing again after an update. To hold a version, set -e DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1. magpie accounts add claude offers it too when Claude Code is missing.

SHELL
Copy
docker exec -it magpie magpie claude-code install

A Grok (SuperGrok) subscription signs in through xAI’s Grok Build CLI, which the image doesn’t have either. Its sign-in, in the browser UI or with magpie plugin login grok, installs it first, as xAI’s installer does: the stable version from x.ai/cli, kept in /config/home/.grok. To use a Grok Build binary you put on the volume yourself, set GROK_BIN_DIR to the folder holding it.

MCP servers

The Library’s MCP servers run in the container, and the image has what they start with: npx, node and npm (Node 24), and uvx, uv, python and python3. A server started with uvx or python downloads its Python into the volume the first time, which takes a few seconds. A server started with docker doesn’t run: the container has no Docker of its own.

The image has no browser. Chrome DevTools’ and Playwright’s MCP servers start a Chrome of their own, so in the container their row in the Library says no Chrome here. Use Magpie Browser instead, which acts in your own browser, or point the server at a Chrome it can reach: --browserUrl http://host:9222 for Chrome DevTools, --cdp-endpoint for Playwright.

An app on the host or another machine reaches the MCP router from outside the container. With a gateway key that has a model, account or spend limit, it is given only the Library’s URL servers, not the ones the container runs as programs (npx, uvx and the like). Give it a key with no such limit to get those too; the router tells the app which servers it left out and why (From another computer).

Your own browser

Magpie Browser lets agents act in your own browser, through its extension. The extension can’t be loaded from the container’s folders, so in the browser UI open Library → Magpie Browser and click Download the extension. The zip is pointed at the page’s own address, with a gateway key named Magpie Browser of its own. Unzip it, open chrome://extensions, turn on Developer mode and click Load unpacked on the unzipped folder. An extension already loaded takes the address (http://localhost:3430, or the gateway’s published port) and a gateway key in its popup.

The Magpie Browser key connects the extension and nothing else: it can’t use models, MCP servers or stats, so a copy of the zip left in Downloads spends nothing. The host’s browser reaches the container from Docker’s bridge, not from the container’s own computer, so it is that key’s alone and the container’s agents don’t use it yet (#5529). To use it from an agent on the host, give that agent a gateway key of its own with full access, connect the extension with the same key in its popup, and call /mcp/magpie/browser with it. A browser given another key is that key’s alone, and it is let go once its key is turned off, removed or rotated.

What is kept

Everything magpie writes is under /config, so a restart, or a new container on the same volume, keeps your providers, keys, sign-ins and plugins.

Path	Holds
/config/magpie	magpie’s own files: settings.json, providers, gateway keys, routing groups
/config/home	the container’s HOME: sign-ins kept where their agent keeps them (~/.codex, ~/.claude…)
/config/cache	the model catalog, Bun, which plugins run on (downloaded the first time one is used), and the Claude Code magpie claude-code install downloaded
/config/data, /config/state	the rest of what magpie keeps

A volume made by an older image keeps working: magpie adds the folders it lacks when it starts. Only sign-ins made with that older image, which lived outside the volume, have to be made again.

Environment
Variable	What it does
MAGPIE_ADDR	where the gateway listens. The image sets 0.0.0.0:3425, so the published port reaches it.
MAGPIE_PUBLIC_URL	the address other machines reach the gateway at, such as http://192.168.1.20:3425 (the host’s or the NAS’s, on the published port), or a reverse proxy’s base URL. In the container magpie sees only Docker’s own 172.17.x address; with this set, the address it shows and prints is the one to use.
MAGPIE_WEB_KEY	the browser UI’s key, kept across restarts (16+ characters)
MAGPIE_NAME	what this magpie is called: the browser tab’s title reads <name> · magpie, to tell several deployments apart. A name set on the page, in Settings → Network and sharing → Advanced → Name, comes first.
MAGPIE_TLS_CERT, MAGPIE_TLS_KEY	a PEM certificate (its chain after it) and its key, mounted into the container: other machines then reach the gateway and the browser UI over https:// only, and plain HTTP from them gets 400. The files are read again when they change, so a renewal needs no restart. One without the other, or files that don’t load, stop magpie from starting. Use https:// in MAGPIE_PUBLIC_URL too.
MAGPIE_ALLOW_IPS	the only addresses other machines may reach the gateway and the browser UI from, as IPs and CIDR ranges: 203.0.113.7,10.0.0.0/8,2001:db8::/32. Any other address gets 403, even with a gateway key. Unset lets every address in, each with a key. See Allowed addresses.
MAGPIE_DRAIN	how long a stop waits for the requests in flight, streams included: seconds (300) or a duration (5m); 20 seconds in Kubernetes and 7 elsewhere unless set (docker stop waits 10), 0 for 2. Past 10, give Docker as long: docker stop -t, Compose’s stop_grace_period. See Kubernetes.
HOME, XDG_CONFIG_HOME, XDG_CACHE_HOME, XDG_DATA_HOME, XDG_STATE_HOME	set by the image to the folders under /config above; leave them
Gateway keys and other machines
Make a key for each client
Gateway → Gateway keys, or in a terminal docker exec magpie magpie gateway-key add "Laptop", which prints the new sk-magpie-key-…. Every request from outside the container, the host’s own included, must carry an enabled gateway key, and one without gets 401. A key can have its own daily, weekly, monthly, every-N-days or every-N-hours limit and its own list of models (magpie gateway-key limit, magpie gateway-key models).
Publish the port
Recreate the container with -p 3425:3425, or bound to the NAS’s LAN or VPN address (-p 192.168.1.20:3425:3425), and with -e MAGPIE_PUBLIC_URL=http://192.168.1.20:3425.

CONTENTS
How it fits together

DOCS · GUIDE

Get started

magpie is one place to choose the model each of your agents uses. Add the providers you have, then pick a model per agent; magpie writes it into that agent’s own config.

Behind it is a small gateway on your machine, at 127.0.0.1:3425. It speaks the OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini APIs and translates between them, streaming and tool calls included, so any agent can use any provider’s models: Claude Code on a GPT model from your ChatGPT plan, Codex on DeepSeek, OpenCode on your Claude plan.

Providers

Where models come from: subscriptions you sign in to, vendors you have an API key for, and your own endpoints. Each model is named provider/model.

Agents

The tools that use them: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode and the rest. One row each, with the model it is set to.

Gateway

The local endpoint every agent is pointed at when you pick a model through magpie. It sends each request to whoever serves that model.

Routing groups

Optional. Several models or accounts an agent picks as one, group/<id>, for when one runs out of quota.

Add providers
Sign in to your subscriptions, paste API keys. Once is enough.
Pick a model for each agent
Click the agent’s model, choose one. magpie rewrites that agent’s config.
Start a new session
Agents read their config when they start; the next session uses the new model.
1 · Add your providers

Open the Providers tab and press ＋ Add provider. Pick a tile, or type a vendor’s name to find it.

Add provider: sign in to a subscription, pick a vendor, or point at any compatible URL.
Subscriptions · sign in, no key

Claude (Pro, Max, Team), ChatGPT (Plus, Pro, Business), Copilot, Gemini (Code Assist) and Antigravity; Cursor, Grok (SuperGrok), Devin and others are added from the Plugins page. Click the tile and magpie opens the vendor’s own sign-in page in your browser; the account shows up as soon as you finish (Copilot gives you a code to enter on GitHub’s page). Subscriptions are added here, in magpie, not by logging in inside another agent.

More than one account. Click the Claude or ChatGPT tile again to add another; each is listed under the provider, one click from being the one in use.
Already signed in? An agent you are signed in to on this machine shows up as a provider too, signed in as ….
Every agent can use it. A subscription’s models are claude/…, codex/…, copilot/…, antigravity/… in every other agent’s picker: to run Antigravity’s Claude or Gemini models in Codex or Claude Code, sign in to Antigravity here and pick an antigravity/… model on the agent’s row. Nothing else to set up. Google may suspend an Antigravity account it sees used outside Antigravity, so use one you can afford to lose. Claude subscription requests run through the Claude Code installed on this machine, so keep it installed.
Vendors

Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi, Zhipu GLM, MiniMax, Qwen, Mistral, Groq, xAI and more. Pick one, paste the key (Get a key ↗ links to the vendor’s key page), save. magpie asks the vendor which models it serves and offers those; open the provider’s row to choose which ones agents see, or Test it.

On this machine

Ollama and LM Studio. No key.

Custom · any compatible URL

For anything else: a Name, an OpenAI compatible base URL (ending in /v1), an Anthropic compatible one (the root, what ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL would take), or both, and the key. Give every API the endpoint speaks; each agent uses the one it speaks natively and magpie translates for the rest.

Already set up providers in Claude Code or Codex? Import… at the top of the sheet reads Claude Code’s settings.json and Codex’s config.toml, changes nothing in them, and brings over the providers you tick.

Keys live in ~/.config/magpie/providers.json, readable by you alone. magpie never reads keys from your shell environment: what you add is what it uses.

2 · Pick a model for each agent

The Agents tab has a row for each agent installed or configured on this machine. magpie knows Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, MiMo Code, DevEco Code, Pi, Goose, Cursor CLI, Copilot CLI, Crush, DeepSeek Harness, Command Code, omp, OmO, Devin, Hermes Agent, MiniMax Code, Grok Build, ZCode, OpenHanako and Alma.

One row per agent. Pick a model from any provider; profiles switch everything at once.
Click the model to open the picker. Models are grouped: the agent’s own, your routing groups, then each provider you added. Type to filter, or type any model id that is not listed.
Reasoning effort, where the agent has it (Codex’s effort, Pi’s thinking), is a slider under the list.
Fast mode. A model with a fast mode has a bolt on its row, beside its star; it shows on the picked row and under the pointer. That is a GPT model of a ChatGPT (Codex) account, a GPT or o-series model on an OpenAI key, Cursor’s models with a fast variant, Claude Opus on an Anthropic key, and a plugin’s or another magpie’s model that says it is served at priority. Click it, and every request this agent sends that model goes in its vendor’s fast mode, quicker at a higher price: service_tier: "priority", as Codex’s own /fast sends it, or Claude’s speed: "fast", whatever API the agent speaks. Click again for Ultrafast, where a ChatGPT account offers it on the model, and again for the usual speed. Each agent is switched apart, and the model’s fallbacks go as they are. In a routing group, each member has the same switch in its row.
Claude Code through magpie can also give its opus, sonnet and haiku tiers models of their own; by default they follow the main model.

Picking a model writes it into the agent’s own config file. Only the keys magpie needs change; comments, ordering and indentation survive, and writes are atomic.

Agent	What a model through magpie writes
Claude Code	~/.claude/settings.json: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and the model variables in its env block
Codex	~/.codex/config.toml: a [model_providers.magpie] table and the model, with the list in magpie-models.json. Your ChatGPT sign-in is left alone
OpenCode, MiMo Code, DevEco Code, Pi, Crush	A magpie provider entry, and magpie/provider/model
Open Code Review	~/.opencodereview/config.json: a magpie custom provider, made the one ocr uses
Kigi	~/.kigi/config.toml: a [model."magpie/…"] table per model, the one picked made the default
AtomCode	~/.atomcode/config.toml: a magpie provider account and one model entry per catalog model
Snow CLI	~/.snow/profiles/magpie.json: a magpie profile, made the active one (Snow App takes it in with "Sync Snow CLI API config")
QwenPaw	A magpie provider in ~/.qwenpaw.secret/providers/custom/magpie.json, and each agent's active_model in its agent.json. Restart QwenPaw after the first connect
Gemini CLI	GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL pointed at the gateway, API-key auth, and the model

A running session keeps the model it started with. Agents read their config when they start, so the change applies to the next session. Codex builds its model list at start-up too: restart the Codex app and open codex sessions after a switch.

Paseo, editor extensions and other front-ends that run Claude Code or Codex for you start the same CLI, which reads the same ~/.claude or ~/.codex config. Set the model once in magpie and they get it too, from their next session.
claude-magpie: Claude Code through magpie, claude left as it is. To keep a plain claude on your own Claude account and start magpie's Claude Code only when you ask for it, leave Claude Code unconnected and run claude-magpie instead. It starts the same claude with magpie's settings over yours for that session (the gateway, the model and its tiers), so ~/.claude/settings.json is never rewritten. Every argument goes to Claude Code: claude-magpie --resume, claude-magpie -p "…". magpie puts it beside the magpie command when you add that in Settings › Command line; with the command there already, run magpie claude launcher add once. magpie claude run does the same. A model you pick with /model in it is kept for the next claude-magpie, and your own claude keeps its model. magpie has to be running.
3 · Optional: routing groups

With one account per provider you can skip this. It matters once you have several: two ChatGPT accounts, or the same model from a subscription and from a key.

Routing groups: several models or accounts behind one name, with smart or ordered fallback.
Several accounts or keys in one provider

Open the provider’s row and tick every account or key to use. Routing says how requests spread over them: Smart (the default), In order, Until used up, staying on the next once one is used up even after the first renews, In turn, Least used first, Use before expiry, By weight, each account or key taking its share by the weight set beside it (a Max account 5, a Pro one 1), or Speed first, the key that answered fastest lately first. Fallback lists models to use instead when the provider is out of quota, rate limited or down.

One model over several providers

A group is several models, from one provider or many, that an agent picks as one: group/<id>, under Routing groups in the picker. A model two of your providers serve under the same name becomes a group on its own; New group in the Routing tab makes one of any models you like. The first model answers for what the group can do.

Groups you get without doing anything. Add a second provider that serves a model you already have — Claude Opus from your Claude subscription and from Copilot, DeepSeek from its own API and from OpenRouter — and magpie makes it a group by itself, auto/<model> (the model's own id, as in auto/claude-opus-4.6; the older group/auto-… id still works), over every provider that serves it. The name is matched however each vendor spells it (deepseek/deepseek-chat, deepseek-chat). Pick it for an agent to spread its requests over all of them; magpie group rm hides one you don’t want.
One model under the provider's odd id. Some providers serve a model under an id of their own, deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 or grok-4.6@500k. Give it the id you want in the provider's editor, under Names, prices & levels, in Listed as beside Same as, then Save; or run magpie model id relay/grok-4.6@500k grok-4.6. magpie then lists it, routes it, joins it to the auto/grok-4.6 group with your other providers' grok-4.6, holds gateway keys to it and counts its usage as grok-4.6, and still asks the provider for grok-4.6@500k. One id is one model of a provider: the last one you give it to has it, and the provider's own model of that id is left out of the list while it does. magpie model id relay/grok-4.6 --reset takes it back, and magpie model ids lists them. It works for a subscription you signed in to and a plugin's provider too (magpie model id cursor/deepseek-v41-flash-1017 deepseek-v4.1-flash): the account or the plugin is still asked for its own id.
Routing	What goes first
Smart smart	The default. Over the members’ accounts and keys together (a group in the group as one, see below): of the subscriptions with quota to spare, the one whose allowance renews soonest. The week decides; an account with five hours and no week (Claude Enterprise) goes by its five hours, so ahead of every week renewing later. Credits with no reset (WorkBuddy’s packages, each ending on its own day) count as renewing when the soonest of those left run out, so the WorkBuddy account whose credits end first goes first; accounts renewing together (free ones at the month’s end) go by whose credits left end first after that. One resting after a failure goes last.
In order order	The first model until it can’t answer, then the next.
Until used up drain	One account or key until it is used up, then the next, which keeps the requests: one before it that renews meanwhile doesn’t take them back. One rate limited or failing is passed over only while it rests.
Before expiry, one by one pace-drain	The account with the most of its allowance left per hour until it is lost, as Use before expiry p

Quickstart

Run LiteLLM and PostgreSQL locally, then use the Admin UI to add models, create keys, and send your first request.

Up and running in a minute

macOS/Linux
Windows
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/main/litellm/scripts/quickstart.sh | sh

When the command finishes, open the Admin UI. Then you can add your models, create virtual keys, and call the gateway from your apps.

Copy agent prompt
1. Start LiteLLM​
curl -sSLO https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/raw/main/litellm/deploy/docker/docker-compose.quickstart.yml
printf 'LITELLM_MASTER_KEY=sk-%s\nLITELLM_SALT_KEY=sk-%s\n' "$(openssl rand -hex 32)" "$(openssl rand -hex 32)" > .env
docker compose -f docker-compose.quickstart.yml up -d

The compose file starts the full LiteLLM proxy on port 4000 and PostgreSQL. Pin a tested release tag or digest before production.

For Kubernetes, see the Helm guide.

Cloud deployment options

Railway and Render host the same gateway and Postgres for you. For AWS and GCP, use the Terraform deployment guide. Use your deployment's URL wherever this guide says http://localhost:4000.

On Render, set Blueprint Path to litellm/deploy/render/render.yaml after signing in, before you deploy.

What the two keys do

The local setup generates both keys in .env. The compose file requires both keys. On a 1-click deploy, set them in the provider's environment.

LITELLM_MASTER_KEY authorizes every management API call and serves as the default Admin UI password. The generated sk- prefix is optional.

LITELLM_SALT_KEY encrypts the provider API keys you add in the UI. It has no in-place rotation, so keep the generated value: changing it later makes every stored credential unreadable until you re-enter it. See key rotations for how the two keys relate.

2. Log in to the Admin UI​

Open http://localhost:4000/ui. The username is admin and the password is the LITELLM_MASTER_KEY value in .env.

3. Add your first model​

Go to Models + Endpoints, open the Add Model tab, pick your provider and models, and paste your provider API key.

Click Test Connect to verify the key against the provider, then Add Model. It appears under Deployed Models with its pricing already mapped:

Keep provider keys out of the UI

If you prefer to manage provider keys as environment variables, download the compose file, add them to the litellm service (for example OPENAI_API_KEY: ${OPENAI_API_KEY}), and enter os.environ/OPENAI_API_KEY in the API key field instead of the raw key.

4. Send a test message​

Go to Playground, select your model, and send a message. The response includes latency and token counts:

The Get Code button generates the equivalent API call for your language.

5. Create a virtual key​

Virtual keys are what you hand to applications and teammates instead of raw provider keys. Each key can carry its own budget, rate limits, and model access, and all its spend is tracked automatically.

Go to Virtual Keys, click + Create New Key, give it a name, and click Create Key:

Copy the key now. It is shown only once.

6. Call the gateway from your app​

The gateway is OpenAI-compatible, so any OpenAI SDK works by pointing it at http://localhost:4000 with your virtual key.

curl
OpenAI Python SDK
OpenAI JS SDK
curl http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer sk-<your-virtual-key>' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "gpt-6.1-sol",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in five words."}]
  }'

Expected response:

{
  "id": "chatcmpl-DzGKiNRbQ4fe9Mgt8HSHFQ6ApfRJi",
  "model": "gpt-6.1-sol",
  "object": "chat.completion",
  "choices": [
    {
      "finish_reason": "stop",
      "index": 0,
      "message": {
        "content": "Hello, nice to meet you.",
        "role": "assistant"
      }
    }
  ],
  "usage": {
    "completion_tokens": 70,
    "prompt_tokens": 12,
    "total_tokens": 82
  }
}

The whole flow, end to end​
Running without a database​

For API access without database-backed model management, virtual keys, or spend tracking, run the same image with a config file:

# litellm_config.yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: gpt-6.1-sol
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/gpt-6.1-sol
      api_key: os.environ/OPENAI_API_KEY

export OPENAI_API_KEY="<your-openai-key>"
export LITELLM_MASTER_KEY="sk-<paste-a-long-random-key>"

docker run \
  -v "$PWD/litellm_config.yaml:/app/config.yaml:ro" \
  -e OPENAI_API_KEY \
  -e LITELLM_MASTER_KEY \
  -p 127.0.0.1:4000:4000 \
  docker.litellm.ai/berriai/litellm:latest \
  --config /app/config.yaml

Requests authenticate with the master key. See the full config reference for everything the file supports.

Budgets are not enforced without a database

litellm_settings.max_budget requires a database to load spend and enforce the global budget. Without one, max_budget: 100 keeps serving requests past $100 with no request error or budget alert. The proxy logs a one-time warning at startup.

Virtual keys also require a database. Requests that carry one fail with No connected db.. The master key has no budget of its own.

To enforce LiteLLM budgets, run with a database. Otherwise, configure spending limits at your provider.

Next steps​

Use the deployment guides for Helm and Terraform, and the production checklist for hardening and tuning. The repository's docker-compose.yml includes database, Redis, and Prometheus options.
